description: Anticipated uncertain threat and perceived danger can shade into each other.
conditions: Semantic proximity in self-reported responses to evocative videos in Cowen and Keltner (2017); this is not evidence of a temporal transition.
counterexamples: Anxiety can remain diffuse without immediate fear.

description: Fear and horror occupy nearby parts of the reported emotion space in this study.
conditions: A frightening event is also deeply disturbing.
counterexamples: Fear of a routine risk need not involve horror.

description: Horror and disgust can overlap in responses to aversive scenes.
conditions: A scene is both disturbing and repellent.
counterexamples: Horror need not involve contamination or revulsion.

description: Enjoyment can include playful humor.
conditions: A welcome event is funny.
counterexamples: Joy need not involve laughter.

description: Pleasant engagement can have an energized quality.
conditions: A valued opportunity is unfolding.
counterexamples: Quiet joy can lack excitement.

description: Pleasure can include a sense of enoughness.
conditions: The present feels welcome and sufficient.
counterexamples: Excited joy may involve wanting more.

description: Satisfaction and settled activation can coincide.
conditions: Demands feel manageable.
counterexamples: A calm person may be dissatisfied.

description: Sorrow can be part of responding to loss.
conditions: Something deeply valued is lost.
counterexamples: Sadness need not be grief.

description: An unmet expectation can carry sorrow.
conditions: A hoped-for result does not arrive.
counterexamples: Disappointment may instead feel irritated.

description: Obstruction can be experienced as both anger and frustration.
conditions: A blocked goal feels unfair.
counterexamples: Frustration can remain non-angry.

description: An immediate grievance can resemble a persistent one.
conditions: An offense remains salient.
counterexamples: Anger can end without resentment.

description: Both can involve strong opposition.
conditions: Anger broadens into rejection of its target.
counterexamples: A person can be angry with someone they love.

description: Readiness for annoyance can accompany anger.
conditions: Several small irritants accumulate.
counterexamples: Irritability need not target anyone.

description: Revulsion and disdain can overlap in moral judgment.
conditions: Conduct is judged repellent and beneath respect.
counterexamples: Physical disgust need not involve contempt.

description: Both can accompany a perceived failing, with different evaluative focus.
conditions: A person judges both self and action negatively.
counterexamples: Guilt can be specific without global self-condemnation.

description: Both can involve uncomfortable self-consciousness.
conditions: Unwanted attention feels exposing.
counterexamples: Embarrassment can be light and brief.

description: A judged harmful choice can also evoke wishing one had chosen differently.
conditions: An action harmed someone.
counterexamples: Regret can concern a harmless missed opportunity.

description: Both can accompany an unwanted outcome.
conditions: A choice produced less than hoped.
counterexamples: Disappointment need not involve self-attributed choice.

description: Care for someone can include concern about their suffering.
conditions: A loved person is struggling.
counterexamples: Love can occur without present suffering.

description: Affection and goodwill share a caring orientation.
conditions: One wishes another well.
counterexamples: Goodwill need not involve close attachment.

description: Concern for suffering and wishes for well-being can overlap.
conditions: A person needs care.
counterexamples: Goodwill can occur without perceived distress.

description: Concern for suffering may feel sorrowful.
conditions: Another's pain is vivid.
counterexamples: Compassion can be steady rather than sad.

description: Settled attention may accompany balanced engagement.
conditions: Experience is met without strong reactivity.
counterexamples: Equanimity can coexist with bodily activation.

description: Balance can accompany acknowledgment of reality.
conditions: An unwanted fact is recognized.
counterexamples: Acceptance can occur with intense distress.

description: Deliberate steadiness may support both qualities.
conditions: Delay or difficulty is present.
counterexamples: Patience can be effortful and emotionally stirred.

description: Achievement can feel both satisfying and joyful.
conditions: A personally meaningful effort succeeds.
counterexamples: Joy need not involve achievement.

description: Appreciation can include warmth toward a benefactor.
conditions: Support is received within a caring relationship.
counterexamples: Gratitude need not involve attachment.

description: Comparison and threatened belonging can be confused or overlap.
conditions: A rival has something valued.
counterexamples: Envy need not threaten an existing relationship.

description: Wonder and appreciation of excellence may overlap.
conditions: An extraordinary skill is witnessed.
counterexamples: Awe can arise without an admirable agent.

description: An information gap can be both puzzling and engaging.
conditions: Understanding seems attainable.
counterexamples: Confusion can block curiosity.

description: Unsatisfying engagement can be frustrating.
conditions: Task autonomy is low.
counterexamples: Boredom can remain passive without frustration.

description: Demand overload can coexist with anticipation of difficulty.
conditions: Several uncertain demands compete.
counterexamples: Overwhelm can occur without future-oriented worry.

description: Remembering valued times can combine pleasure and ache.
conditions: A remembered period is cherished and gone.
counterexamples: Nostalgia may be mostly pleasant.

description: Release of pressure can be followed by settling.
conditions: A burden appears to have ended.
counterexamples: Relief can be excited or short-lived.

description: Pleasantness versus sorrow is a useful valence contrast. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: Both refer to the same event or interval.
counterexamples: They can coexist in bittersweet experience.

description: Perceived possibility contrasts with felt absence of a way forward. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: The same valued outcome is considered.
counterexamples: Hope and despair can alternate or concern different outcomes.

description: Settled activation contrasts with apprehensive activation. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: Compare the level of felt agitation.
counterexamples: A person can be outwardly calm while anxious.

description: Felt sufficiency contrasts with painful comparison. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: Attention concerns what one has relative to another.
counterexamples: One can feel content in one domain and envious in another.

description: Concern at suffering contrasts with pleasure at another's misfortune. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: The same person's setback is the focus.
counterexamples: Mixed responses to the same event are possible.

description: Gladness for another's benefit contrasts with pain at their advantage. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: Another's success is the focus.
counterexamples: A person can feel both at once.

description: Goodwill contrasts with strong rejection or hostility. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: The same target is considered.
counterexamples: Goodwill can coexist with opposition to harmful conduct.

description: Deliberate non-retaliation contrasts with an urge to react against an offense. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: An offense or obstruction is being met.
counterexamples: Patience does not require anger to be absent.

description: Engaged inquiry contrasts with unsatisfying engagement. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: The same activity is being considered.
counterexamples: A person may be bored with a task and curious about its purpose.

description: Acknowledging reality contrasts with continuing grievance in one possible dimension. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: The person is considering an unresolved event.
counterexamples: Acceptance can coexist with a demand for justice.

description: Available settled feeling differs from muted access to feeling despite superficial quietness. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: Both appear externally inactive.
counterexamples: Low visible expression does not distinguish either state.

description: Respect for excellence contrasts with disdain. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: Evaluations concern the same target.
counterexamples: Someone can admire a skill while disdaining conduct.

description: Easing of perceived threat contrasts with its felt presence. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: A particular danger is evaluated.
counterexamples: Relief about one danger can coexist with fear about another.

description: Positive and painful self-evaluation can contrast. This is a specified contrast, not a universal opposite or antidote.
conditions: One aspect of self or conduct is evaluated.
counterexamples: Both can coexist about different aspects of an event.

description: Apprehension may become more immediate fear.
conditions: An uncertain threat seems imminent.
counterexamples: New information may instead reduce threat.

description: Fear may ease into relief.
conditions: A perceived threat credibly passes.
counterexamples: The person may remain vigilant after danger ends.

description: An unresolved concern may ease.
conditions: A consequential uncertainty is resolved favorably.
counterexamples: Reassurance may be unconvincing or incomplete.

description: Anger may give way to sorrow.
conditions: Attention shifts from the offense to what was lost.
counterexamples: Anger and sadness may persist together.

description: Threat may be met with mobilized protest.
conditions: The person perceives a possible boundary defense.
counterexamples: Fear may instead lead to withdrawal.

description: Blocked effort may become angry protest.
conditions: Obstruction is interpreted as unfair or intentional.
counterexamples: The obstacle may be treated as impersonal.

description: Frustration may ease when progress resumes.
conditions: A workable route becomes available.
counterexamples: Exhaustion or resentment may remain.

description: An unresolved offense may become a lasting grievance.
conditions: The event is repeatedly revisited without resolution.
counterexamples: Anger may dissipate without lasting grievance.

description: A lingering grievance may become acutely activated.
conditions: A reminder or repeated offense occurs.
counterexamples: A reminder may instead bring sadness or little feeling.

description: Painful self-evaluation may be followed by defensive anger.
conditions: Attention shifts toward blame or perceived humiliation.
counterexamples: Shame can lead to withdrawal without anger.

description: Global self-condemnation may narrow to concern about an action.
conditions: The person distinguishes conduct from their entire identity.
counterexamples: The self-condemnation may persist.

description: Guilt may ease after a meaningful repair.
conditions: Responsibility is acknowledged and repair feels adequate.
counterexamples: Repair may not be possible or sufficient.

description: Counterfactual dwelling may shift toward acknowledgment.
conditions: Attention turns to the limits of changing the past.
counterexamples: Acceptance may coexist with continuing regret.

description: An unmet hope may become sorrow.
conditions: The loss of the hoped-for outcome becomes salient.
counterexamples: Disappointment can instead mobilize renewed effort.

description: An unmet expectation may be followed by renewed possibility.
conditions: A credible alternative appears.
counterexamples: Alternatives may not address the original loss.

description: Hope may change when a desired outcome fails.
conditions: Evidence contradicts the hoped-for result.
counterexamples: Hope may persist or move to another outcome.

description: A felt lack of options may shift toward possibility.
conditions: A credible option or supportive connection becomes available.
counterexamples: A suggestion alone may feel irrelevant or overwhelming.

description: Disconnection may ease with meaningful contact.
conditions: The contact feels welcome and understanding.
counterexamples: Unwanted or superficial contact may deepen loneliness.

description: Painful comparison may shift toward appreciation.
conditions: Attention moves from relative disadvantage to valued skill.
counterexamples: Comparison may continue to feel threatening.

description: Envy may precede pleasure at a rival's setback.
conditions: The envy includes wishing to diminish the rival.
counterexamples: Envy oriented toward self-improvement need not do so.

description: Not understanding may become inviting exploration.
conditions: The gap feels manageable and safe to investigate.
counterexamples: Overload or threat may prevent engagement.

description: Unclear information may become distressing obstruction.
conditions: Repeated attempts to understand fail.
counterexamples: The uncertainty may remain enjoyable.

description: Unsatisfying engagement may shift toward interest.
conditions: A meaningful question or novel feature becomes apparent.
counterexamples: Novelty may fail to engage.

description: Excess demand may become more manageable.
conditions: Load is reduced or useful support arrives.
counterexamples: The person may need time to recover.

description: Readiness for annoyance may settle.
conditions: Discomfort or demands lessen and rest becomes available.
counterexamples: A deeper unresolved concern may remain.

description: Energized expectation may fall into disappointment.
conditions: An anticipated experience does not materialize.
counterexamples: The person may feel neutral or adapt quickly.

description: Present enjoyment may become fond longing in memory.
conditions: A meaningful period has ended.
counterexamples: Remembrance need not include longing.

description: Loss may bring appreciation alongside sorrow.
conditions: A valued memory or past kindness comes to mind.
counterexamples: Gratitude is not required and does not erase grief.

description: Easing can itself become a focus of self-judgment.
conditions: A person believes relief after loss is disloyal.
counterexamples: Relief can be accepted without guilt.

description: Social discomfort may soften into shared humor.
conditions: The situation feels safe and laughter is welcome.
counterexamples: Teasing can intensify embarrassment.

description: Achievement satisfaction may widen to appreciation.
conditions: Contributions from others become salient.
counterexamples: Pride need not disappear or turn into gratitude.

description: Pleasure at misfortune may be followed by moral discomfort.
conditions: The person notices a conflict with their values.
counterexamples: They may regard the misfortune as deserved.

description: Disdain may shift toward concern.
conditions: The target's vulnerability becomes salient.
counterexamples: Understanding someone does not necessarily change disdain.

description: Goodwill toward an annoying person is described as a traditional practice association.
conditions: In the contemplative context of AN 5.161.
counterexamples: This is not a guaranteed sequence, demand, or instruction for an outside agent to induce.

description: Concern for an annoying person’s suffering is described as a traditional practice association.
conditions: In the contemplative context of AN 5.161.
counterexamples: This is not a guaranteed sequence, demand, or instruction for an outside agent to induce.

description: Balanced regard is described as a traditional practice association with less annoyance.
conditions: In the contemplative context of AN 5.161.
counterexamples: This is not a guaranteed sequence, demand, or instruction for an outside agent to induce.

description: Cultivated patience is traditionally described in relation to meeting anger.
conditions: In the ethical and contemplative context of Shantideva’s chapter on patience.
counterexamples: Anger may persist; patience does not imply accepting abuse.

description: Pleasant and painful feelings can coexist.
conditions: A meaningful ending is both welcome and a loss.
counterexamples: Many events evoke only one of these states.

description: Desire for an outcome can coexist with apprehension.
conditions: A valued result remains uncertain.
counterexamples: Hope can be calm rather than anxious.

description: Care and anger can concern the same person.
conditions: A loved person violates a boundary.
counterexamples: Anger does not establish love or its absence.

description: Loss can coexist with release of a burden.
conditions: A loss also ends strain or suffering.
counterexamples: Many losses involve no relief.

description: Concern can coexist with balanced attention.
conditions: Suffering is met with steady care.
counterexamples: Apparent composure can also reflect detachment.

description: Gladness for someone can coexist with painful comparison.
conditions: A friend receives a desired opportunity.
counterexamples: Either feeling may occur alone.

description: Different evaluations can coexist.
conditions: An achievement is connected with conduct the person regrets.
counterexamples: The evaluations may instead alternate.

description: Appreciation can coexist with sorrow.
conditions: A kindness arrives during a difficult loss.
counterexamples: Gratitude does not require sorrow.

description: Acknowledgment and protest can coexist.
conditions: Reality is recognized while unfairness remains objectionable.
counterexamples: Acceptance can occur without anger.

description: Remembered connection can accompany present disconnection.
conditions: A cherished social world feels unavailable.
counterexamples: Nostalgia can also strengthen present connection.

description: Exploration and threat can coexist.
conditions: An unfamiliar thing seems both interesting and risky.
counterexamples: Fear may suppress exploration entirely.

description: Low engagement can coincide with annoyance.
conditions: A repetitive task is difficult to leave.
counterexamples: Boredom need not involve irritability.
